headline: U.S. prices rise faster than expected in October

sources.title: US inflation higher than expected in October - here's what is happening with prices (BBC)
Gas prices dip below $4 but inflation stays stubbornly high (NPR)
US inflation rose more than expected last month (CNN)

chunks.text: U.S. drivers got some good news at the gas pump in November 2026. On November 10, the [[average price]] of regular gas was 3.98 dollars a [[gallon]], according to the American Automobile Association. The price had {{come down}} 38 cents in a month. It was under 4 dollars for the first time in three months. Higher rents and food prices {{drove up}} the [[cost of living]] in October.

verbs.wrong: To change from day to day
verbs.why: The price of a new phone comes down after a few months. Strawberries come down in price every summer. The price of regular gas had come down 38 cents in a month.
Bad weather drives up the price of fruit. Big concerts drive up hotel prices downtown. Higher rents and food prices drove up the cost of living in October.

chunks.text: On November 10, the Labor Department said [[consumer prices]], the prices people pay for everyday things, rose 0.4 percent in October. Economists had expected 0.3 percent. Rent and other [[housing costs]] {{made up}} about a third of the [[monthly increase]]. Food prices rose 0.5 percent. Economists say high [[diesel]] prices likely make trucking food more expensive. Many businesses {{pass those costs on}} to shoppers. Baby food and [[baby formula]] {{stood out}}, with prices up 5.1 percent.

verbs.correct: To form a part of a total
verbs.why: Rent makes up half of my monthly costs. Women make up most of the nurses at this hospital. Rent and other housing costs made up about a third of the monthly increase.

verbs.correct: To make someone else pay a cost
verbs.wrong: To list a cost on a receipt
verbs.why: Restaurants pass higher food costs on to diners. When fuel gets expensive, airlines pass the cost on to travelers. Many businesses pass the higher cost of trucking food on to shoppers.

verbs.wrong: To be sold only in stores
verbs.why: Her red coat stands out in a crowd. One number on the bill stands out because it is so high. Baby food and baby formula stood out, with prices up 5.1 percent in October.

chunks.text: [[Inflation]] is the rate at which prices rise over time. The monthly report usually also shows how much prices changed over a full year. This time, the report had to {{leave that number out}}. Many federal government offices {{shut down}} in October 2025, so [[price checkers]] did not record prices that month. In the 12 months to September 2026, prices rose 3.7 percent. Economists [[estimate]] the yearly rate for October at close to 4 percent.

verbs.why: This short list leaves out a few names. My brother often leaves out the boring parts of a story. This time, the report had to leave the yearly number out.

verbs.correct: To stop working for a time
verbs.wrong: To vote on a new budget
verbs.why: The museum shuts down for repairs every January. Some schools shut down when it snows a lot. Many government offices shut down in October 2025, so prices were not recorded that month.

chunks.text: Average pay rose only about 3.1 percent over the past year. Rising prices {{eat up}} those [[pay raises]], and many families feel they are {{falling behind}}. The Federal Reserve, the country's [[central bank]], wants inflation of about 2 percent. To {{rein in}} prices, it can raise [[interest rates]], the cost of [[borrowing]] money. When loans cost more, people and businesses usually {{cut back}} on spending. The Federal Reserve raised rates in September 2026, and many economists expect another rise in December.

verbs.correct: To take most or all of something
verbs.wrong: To be given once a year
verbs.why: Rent eats up half of his paycheck. Car repairs eat up all the money we save. Rising prices eat up the pay raises that many workers got over the past year.

verbs.correct: To fail to match rising costs
verbs.wrong: To move to a cheaper home
verbs.why: Many families fall behind when rent rises faster than pay. Older people on small pensions often fall behind as food gets more expensive. Prices are rising faster than pay, so many families feel they are falling behind.

verbs.correct: To control something and stop its growth
verbs.why: The new manager reins in costs at the factory. Our city tries to rein in traffic with higher parking fees. To rein in prices, the Federal Reserve can raise interest rates.

verbs.correct: To reduce the amount of something
verbs.wrong: To pay with a credit card
verbs.why: When money is short, we cut back on movies and coffee. Many shoppers cut back when prices rise. When loans cost more, people and businesses usually cut back on spending.

wordDefs.def: The usual price found by adding prices and dividing by their number
ex: The average price of a movie ticket is about 11 dollars.
We paid more than the average price for our car.
The average price of a cup of coffee in this city is high.

wordDefs.def: A unit for measuring liquid, equal to about 3.8 liters
ex: We buy a gallon of milk every week.
This car can go 40 miles on one gallon of gas.
She drinks half a gallon of water a day.

wordDefs.def: The amount of money people need to pay for basic things like food and rent
ex: The cost of living is very high in big cities.
They moved to a town with a lower cost of living.
Her pay does not match the cost of living.

wordDefs.def: The prices that people pay for goods and services
ex: Consumer prices often rise when fuel gets more expensive.
The government tracks consumer prices every month.
Lower consumer prices help families save money.

wordDefs.def: The money people spend on rent or on owning a home
ex: Housing costs take a big part of a young worker's pay.
Many families moved because housing costs were too high.
Housing costs are lower in small towns.

wordDefs.def: The amount by which something grows in one month
ex: The monthly increase in our electric bill surprised us.
Her savings show a small monthly increase.
The store tracks the monthly increase in sales.

wordDefs.def: A heavy fuel used by trucks, buses and trains
ex: The truck driver stopped to buy diesel.
Diesel costs more than regular gas in many states.
Most large farm machines run on diesel.

wordDefs.def: A powder or liquid that is mixed to feed babies in place of breast milk
ex: She keeps a can of baby formula in the kitchen.
The store had no baby formula on its shelves.
Baby formula can be expensive for new parents.

wordDefs.def: The rise in the prices of goods and services over time
ex: Inflation makes a dollar buy less than before.

wordDefs.def: Workers who visit stores to write down the prices of goods

wordDefs.def: To make a careful guess about a number or amount

wordDefs.def: Increases in the money that workers earn
ex: The nurses asked for pay raises.

wordDefs.def: A country's main bank, which controls its money and interest rates
ex: The central bank raised interest rates to slow rising prices.

The central bank wants prices to stay steady.

wordDefs.def: The cost of borrowing money, shown as a percent of the loan
ex: Low interest rates make it cheaper to buy a house.
Higher interest rates make car loans more expensive.

wordDefs.def: Taking money from a bank or person and paying it back later
ex: Borrowing money for college is common in the U.S.

mainIdea.s: U.S. prices rose more than experts expected in October, led by rent and food costs. Gas got cheaper, but pay is not rising as fast as prices, and interest rates may go higher.
mainIdea.why: Rising rents and food prices drove up the cost of living. Many families feel they are falling behind, and the Federal Reserve may raise rates again in December.

mainIdea.s: A big jump in gas costs pushed American prices well above forecasts during October. Economists now think the central bank will lower borrowing costs in December to help families.
mainIdea.why: Close, but gas prices came down in October and November. Rent and food led the rise, and economists expect the Federal Reserve to raise rates again.

mainIdea.s: A new report says shoppers in the U.S. spent record amounts online during the big October sales. Stores sold more phones and TVs than ever before, mostly to younger buyers.
mainIdea.why: This story is about rising prices in October. Rent and other housing costs made up about a third of the monthly increase.

tf.s: Gas prices came down, but overall consumer prices still rose in October.
tf.why: Regular gas fell by 38 cents in a month, but consumer prices rose 0.4 percent in October.

tf.s: Consumer prices rose less than economists had expected in October.
tf.why: Prices rose more than expected. Higher rents and food prices drove up the cost of living.

tf.s: Rent and other housing costs made up a big part of the October rise.
tf.why: Housing costs made up about a third of the monthly increase.

tf.s: The report left out the usual yearly figure for inflation.
tf.why: The government did not record prices in October 2025, so it had to leave the yearly number out.

tf.s: For the typical worker, pay is rising faster than prices.
tf.why: Pay is rising more slowly than prices, so many families feel they are falling behind.

tf.s: Many economists expect the Federal Reserve to raise rates again in December.
tf.why: The Federal Reserve raised rates in September 2026, and it may raise them again to rein in prices.

lines.text: Did you see that gas prices finally {{came down}}?
I did. It's under four dollars a gallon again.
That's [[small comfort]]. Lots of other things got more expensive in October.
Prices rose 0.4 percent in one month. Rent and food {{drove them up}}.
Rent? [[What else is new?]] My landlord raised mine in the spring.
Housing {{made up}} about a third of the increase. And baby formula really {{stood out}}. It jumped more than five percent.
Wow. Families with babies really [[take a hit]] there.
Diesel is expensive too, so trucking food costs more. Businesses {{pass that on}} to shoppers.
What about the yearly number? Is it close to four percent?
Economists think so, but the report {{left it out}}. Many government offices {{shut down}} in October 2025, so nobody recorded prices that month.
And pay isn't rising that fast, right?
Right. Higher prices {{eat up}} most raises, and a lot of families are {{falling behind}}.
And to [[add insult to injury]], the Federal Reserve may raise interest rates again in December.
To {{rein in}} prices. When loans cost more, people {{cut back}}.
I get it, but loans and credit cards will cost even more.

expressions.def: Used to say that one good thing does not help much when things are bad
ex: A free coffee is small comfort after a two-hour delay.

expressions.def: Used to say that a bad thing keeps happening and is no surprise
ex: The train is late again? What else is new?
My phone bill went up. What else is new?

expressions.def: To lose money or suffer harm because of something
ex: Small shops take a hit when a big store opens nearby.
If you skip sleep, you pay the price the next day.

expressions.def: To make a bad situation even worse
ex: Our flight was late, and to add insult to injury, the airline lost my bag.
